newsitem.title: ITALY: Castro makes a meal of world food summit.
newsitem.headline: Castro makes a meal of world food summit.

text.p: The hottest commodities at the World Food Summit on Saturday were autographs of the gathering's undisputed star: Fidel Castro.

The Cuban leader swept into the summit under a blanket of security, complete with gun-toting bodyguards, and delivered a scathing speech in which he dismissed the meeting for setting shamefully inadequate goals.
His harsh assessment did little to dampen enthusiasm over his presence, which added Caribbean spice to a summit which has otherwise served up much worthy but dull fare.
"Everyone has been saying the same things," said delegate Suzgo Kumwenda of Malawi. "I think he added a lot of life."
After delivering his speech, the dark-suited Castro returned to his seat in the plenary hall between the delegations of Croatia and Cyprus to follow the proceedings.
This proved difficult as dignitary after dignitary approached him to shake hands, exchange pleasantries and ask for autographs.
A line of people, including lower-ranking diplomats and employees of the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) which is hosting the summit, formed in the aisle near his seat.

"It was such a thrill. I was so excited," said FAO employee Jacqueline Daldin, a Canadian, after securing an autograph. "I told him I was planning to go to Cuba next year and he said 'You will be very welcome'."
Feu Rosa, a member of Brazil's Chamber of Deputies, was more sceptical, saying the 70-year-old communist was putting on a vintage performance.
"He always has to be well-seen and centre-stage," he said.
Once out of the plenary hall, Castro's security swooped in, cutting off all access.
Castro had lunch at FAO headquarters with other leaders invited by the agency's director-general Jacques Diouf and then headed out to meet Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi.
Police and bodyguards threw a human shield around Castro as he stepped into his car to leave FAO, watched by staff pressing against the Fascist-era building's first-floor windows.
Castro smiled and nodded to reporters and cameramen who had waited in the rain for several hours to watch him leave, but declined to answer pleas for interviews shouted across barriers.
Summit officials said on Friday they had received 2,100 requests for interviews with Castro.
The Cuban leader's security convoy was by far the largest deployed for the more than 80 heads of state or government attending the five-day summit, which ends on Sunday.
With a helicopter buzzing overhead, Castro swept off into the Rome traffic followed by a van with an armed security agent peering out of the top.
Another gun-toting agent could be seen sitting cross-legged in the back of the van guarding the convoy's rear.
